title: "Choosing a permutation scheme"
bibliography: ../references.bib
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`lagged_protest()` offers three ways of building the null distribution of
the Procrustes statistic *m*²: phase-randomized surrogates
(`permutation = "phase"`, the default), cyclic shifts of the full series
(`permutation = "cyclic"`, optionally with time reversal through `mirror`),
and free permutation of rows (`permutation = "free"`). This article
summarizes a simulation study of the three schemes and turns it into
practical advice. The main points are:

* free permutation should not be used with seasonal or autocorrelated
  series;
* the raw p-value at the optimal lag is liberal whatever the scheme, so the
  global p-value (`fit$p.global`) is the one to report;
* for the global p-value, phase surrogates combine good calibration with high
  power, whereas cyclic shifts are calibrated but have low power;
* no scheme is calibrated when the seasonal period differs from the series
  length unless the series is truncated to whole cycles (argument `period`),
  and strong autocorrelation in short series makes all schemes
  somewhat liberal.

## The simulation study

Series were generated with `simulate_lagged_series()` (see
[Simulating lagged series](simulating-series.html) for how it works): seasonal sinusoids plus
AR(1) noise, with `Y` either independent of `X` (Type I error) or following
`X` with a known lag (power). Each of 983 scenarios was replicated 1000
times. The design crossed:

* series length: 12, 24, 48 and 96 time points;
* number of variables in `X` and `Y`: 2, 5 and 10;
* AR(1) autocorrelation of the noise: 0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9;
* relation between the seasonal period and the series length: one complete
  cycle (period = *n*), several complete annual cycles (period = 12 with
  *n* ≥ 24), an incomplete cycle (period = 0.75 *n*) and no seasonality
  (amplitude 0);
* scheme: phase (199 surrogates), cyclic with and without mirror, and free
  permutation (199 permutations, as a reference).

Lags 0–3 were scanned for *n* = 12 and 0–6 otherwise. The rejection rates
below use α = 0.05; with 1000 replicates, a rate of 0.05 has a 95% binomial
interval of about 0.037–0.064.

```{r data}
cal <- read.csv("calibration_v2.csv")
type1 <- subset(cal, block == "type1")
complete <- subset(type1, period_type != "mismatch")
power <- subset(cal, block == "power")

rate_table <- function(data, by, value) {
  agg <- aggregate(data[[value]], data[c(by, "scheme")], mean)
  wide <- reshape(agg, idvar = by, timevar = "scheme", direction = "wide")
  names(wide) <- sub("^x\\.", "", names(wide))
  wide <- wide[order(wide[[by]]), ]
  rownames(wide) <- NULL
  wide
}
```

## Free permutation

Standard PROTEST permutes rows freely, which assumes that time points are
exchangeable [@jackson1995protest; @perezneto2001protest]. Two independent
seasonal series violate this assumption, because both carry temporal
structure that row permutation destroys [@legendre2002spatial; @manly2020randomization, ch. 10]:

```{r free}
free <- subset(cal, block == "free")
aggregate(cbind(global = global) ~ n, data = free, FUN = mean)
```

The test rejects the null hypothesis in practically every replicate, so
free permutation is kept in the package only as a reference.

## Reporting the optimal lag

The usual way of reading a lag scan is to pick the lag with the smallest
*m*² and report its p-value. That p-value ignores both the number of lags
examined and the fact that the lag was chosen after looking at all of them.
In series spanning complete cycles, it rejected the null far more often than
α under every scheme (the zero for the cyclic scheme without mirror at
*n* = 12 only reflects its 11 shifts, which cannot produce a p-value below
0.083):

```{r optimal}
knitr::kable(rate_table(complete, "n", "opt_sig"), digits = 3,
             caption = "Type I error of the raw p-value at the optimal lag.")
```

The global p-value avoids this. It compares the observed minimum *m*² across
lags with the minimum across lags under each permutation (a max-statistic
test), so it is the p-value of the whole scan-and-select procedure.

## Calibration of the global p-value

With series spanning complete cycles, the global p-value was close to the
nominal level under all three schemes for weak to moderate autocorrelation:

```{r global-ar}
knitr::kable(rate_table(complete, "autocorr", "global"), digits = 3,
             caption = "Type I error of the global p-value by AR(1) autocorrelation.")
```

Strong autocorrelation made all schemes liberal, most of all the phase
scheme. The excess was concentrated in short series and in series with many
variables, and faded with length:

```{r global-strong}
strong <- subset(complete, autocorr >= 0.7)
knitr::kable(rate_table(strong, "n", "global"), digits = 3,
             caption = "Type I error of the global p-value, AR(1) of 0.7 and 0.9.")
knitr::kable(rate_table(strong, "p", "global"), digits = 3,
             caption = "Same, by number of variables.")
```

The cyclic scheme without mirror cannot reject at *n* = 12: its 11 shifts
give a smallest attainable p-value of 1/12 = 0.083.

## Power of the global p-value

The two schemes that respect the temporal structure differ sharply in
power. Shifting `Y` by *s* positions and then applying lag *k* pairs the same
rows as lag *k* + *s* without a shift, so when several lags are scanned some
cyclic permutations reproduce the true alignment at another lag. The null
distribution of the minimum *m*² then contains the signal itself, and the
global p-value loses power. Phase surrogates are new series rather than
shifts of the observed one and do not have this problem
[@ebisuzaki1997]:

```{r power, fig.alt = "Power of the global p-value against series length for the cyclic scheme with mirror and the phase scheme."}
pw <- aggregate(global ~ n + scheme, data = power, FUN = mean)
pw <- reshape(pw, idvar = "n", timevar = "scheme", direction = "wide")
names(pw) <- sub("^global\\.", "", names(pw))
matplot(pw$n, pw[, c("cyclic_mirror", "phase")], type = "b", pch = c(1, 19),
        lty = 1, col = c("grey50", "black"), log = "x", ylim = c(0, 1),
        xaxt = "n", xlab = "Number of time points", ylab = "Power (global p)")
axis(1, at = pw$n)
legend("bottomright", c("cyclic (mirror)", "phase"), pch = c(1, 19),
       col = c("grey50", "black"), bty = "n")
knitr::kable(pw, digits = 3)
```

Both schemes recovered the true lag equally well, because the optimal lag
does not depend on the null distribution:

```{r recovery}
aggregate(opt_true ~ n + scheme, data = power, FUN = mean)
```

## When the period differs from the series length

Both the cyclic and the phase schemes treat the series as periodic with
period *n*. When the series does not close a cycle, all schemes failed:

```{r mismatch}
mismatch <- subset(type1, period_type == "mismatch")
knitr::kable(rate_table(mismatch, "n", "global"), digits = 3,
             caption = "Type I error of the global p-value, period = 0.75 n.")
```

This failure is not specific to a scheme. Two series with the same seasonal
period trace the same trajectory shape in multivariate space, and Procrustes
rotation can superimpose them whatever the phase difference between them.
Concordance between two series sharing a period therefore reflects their
common periodicity unless the null model preserves it, which the cyclic
shift does only when the period equals *n* [@kalyuzhny2020cyclic].

The `period` argument handles this case by truncating both series to whole
cycles before the analysis, for example to the first 18 of 24 monthly samples
of an 18-month cycle. We reran the scenarios above with truncation (same
series, 1000 replicates each), plus a power block:

```{r truncation}
tr <- subset(cal, block == "type1_period")
knitr::kable(rate_table(tr, "autocorr", "global"), digits = 3,
             caption = "Type I error of the global p-value, period = 0.75 n, after truncation to whole cycles.")
pt <- subset(cal, block == "power_period")
knitr::kable(rate_table(pt, "n", "global"), digits = 3,
             caption = "Power of the global p-value after truncation, by original series length.")
```

Truncation brought the Type I error back to the level of series that already
span complete cycles: calibrated up to AR(1) of 0.5, slightly liberal at 0.7
and liberal at 0.9 with the phase scheme. It costs data, and so power: a
series of 12 time points with a period of 9 keeps only 9 rows, and power
fell to about 0.39, against 0.79 for 12 rows spanning a complete cycle; the
cyclic scheme cannot reject at all with 9 rows. It also requires the true
period to be known.

Removing the seasonal component by harmonic regression with the known
period was tested in a smaller simulation (300 replicates per scenario,
phase scheme, *n* = 12–48) and is not offered: it reduced the Type I error
to 0.08–0.13 with AR(1) of 0.3 and to 0.21–0.35 with 0.7, but did not
calibrate the test, and it removes the seasonal signal that is often the
object of the analysis.

## Recommendations

* Use the default `permutation = "phase"` with a large `nperm` (999 or more
  for a test at the 5% level, about 4999 when the 1% level matters;
  @manly2020randomization, pp. 57–59) and a `seed`, and report
  `fit$p.global` for the optimal lag together with the lag profile and the
  continuous measures in `fit$effect` (`Z`, `A` and the corrected RV), which
  are not bounded by the number of permutations.
* Make sure the series spans whole cycles of any seasonal signal; if it does
  not, give the length of the cycle in `period`.
* With short series (*n* ≤ 48) that are strongly autocorrelated, report the
  cyclic result as a conservative check; with `mirror = FALSE` it was the
  least liberal scheme in that range, at the cost of power.
* Do not use `permutation = "free"` for time series.
